---
title: "Synthesis evidence: calculate, compare, explain"
---

Allow 75 minutes for the chemistry questions, plus about 50 minutes for your
Rmd results section. This uses **simulated teaching data**, not an approved
experimental procedure. See [practical work and reporting](../reference/practical.qmd)
for the record and report workflow.

## 1. A short route, with a reason for each step

Propose a route from ethanol to ethyl ethanoate using ethanoic acid as an
intermediate. State the functional-group change at each step and where an
additional ethanol portion is required. Why would a procedure designed to
isolate ethanal not automatically be suitable for the acid target?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked route"}
Oxidise an ethanol portion to ethanoic acid under appropriate oxidation
conditions, then combine the acid with a separate ethanol portion in an
acid-catalysed esterification equilibrium. The first transformation is alcohol
oxidation; the second is acyl substitution. Conditions that stop at or isolate
ethanal serve a different target from conditions permitting further oxidation
to the acid. Reagent identity and work-up would need an approved protocol
before carrying this out experimentally.
:::

## 2. A balanced aspirin amount table

The teaching reaction is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin +
ethanoic acid, with 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry. Supplied masses and molar masses:

| Reagent | Mass / g | Molar mass / (g mol⁻¹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salicylic acid | 1.3812 | 138.12 |
| Acetic anhydride | 1.53135 | 102.09 |

Calculate amount as mass/molar mass. Compare amount divided by stoichiometric
coefficient to identify the limiting reagent. Aspirin molar mass is 180.16
g/mol. Predict the theoretical product mass before using the isolated mass.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Dividing g by g/mol gives mol. One mmol is 0.001 mol. A larger mass does not
necessarily indicate an excess reagent; use the balanced reaction.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked calculation"}
Salicylic acid: 0.01000 mol = 10.00 mmol. Acetic anhydride: 0.01500 mol =
15.00 mmol. With coefficients of one, salicylic acid limits product to
0.01000 mol. The theoretical mass is 0.01000 × 180.16 = 1.8016 g. This is a
stoichiometric upper bound under the assumed desired reaction, not evidence
that all of the starting material actually reacted.
:::

## 3. Isolated yield is not purity

The isolated material weighs 1.20 g. Calculate apparent isolated yield as
`100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g`. Name two ways this mass could
overstate the true mass of product. Would a yield below 100% establish purity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Yield is about 66.6%. Residual solvent, water, starting material or other
impurities could add to the measured mass. A value below 100% does not prove
purity: impure material can still weigh less than the theoretical product.
Conversion measures starting-material consumption; selectivity measures how
much of reacted material follows the desired route. Neither is established
solely by this isolated mass.
:::

## 4. A TLC observation with limits

The solvent front travels 5.0 cm. Starting-material reference and product
reference travel 1.2 and 3.2 cm respectively. The crude sample has two spots
at those same distances under the same conditions. Calculate both Rf values
and give a restrained interpretation. Explain why one spot from the isolate
would still not uniquely identify it or prove purity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Rf values are 0.24 and 0.64. The crude contains at least two detected
components under these conditions, with spots consistent with the references.
Different compounds can co-migrate, and some components can be invisible to
the detection method. Compare spectra and use other suitable evidence rather
than treating Rf as a unique identity code.
:::

## 5. Rmd task: results that update when a mass changes

In the student project, save a results section containing the amount table,
limiting-reagent reasoning, theoretical mass and isolated yield. Reuse code
from the [report guide](../reference/practical.qmd) or adapt this transparent
calculation:

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
theoretical_product_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_mass_g <- theoretical_product_mol * 180.16
isolated_mass_g <- 1.20
isolated_yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
knitr::kable(amounts)
isolated_yield_percent
```

The `amounts.csv` table contains the two starting reagents. If adding product
or solvent rows later, select the relevant starting reagents before `min()`.
Inspect the table and check the units. Write the numerical yield using inline
R in the report, not by typing a second independent copy of the number. Add
your TLC table and an interpretation distinguishing evidence for reaction,
identity and purity. Change the isolated mass to 1.10 g, predict the direction
of change, and Knit again before restoring the original teaching value.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproducibility check"}
At 1.10 g the apparent isolated yield becomes about 61.1%. Every dependent
result should change when knitted. If a copied number remains 66.6%, it is
no longer linked to the saved calculation. Correctness also requires the
right stoichiometry and trustworthy primary observations; automatic updating
alone cannot supply either.
:::

Finish with two sentences stating what the observations support and what
remains uncertain. Optional reading: selected Solomons chapters 8, 12 and 17;
see the [reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd).
